title: Noor and the Songbook
premise: Noor Eriksen, a ghostwriter who vanished from public life after a scandal destroyed their reputation, is hired to write the memoirs of celebrated singer-songwriter Marisol Vance—unaware that Marisol's manager, Dev, is the person Noor once loved and abandoned. When a letter Noor wrote eleven years ago surfaces in Marisol's archives, the past threatens to expose not only Noor's identity but the theft of a song that made Marisol famous—a song Dev quietly knows was Noor's. As the Harvest Festival approaches, Noor must choose between staying invisible or claiming authorship of both the song and their own life. In the end, Noor testifies to the truth at the festival, loses the memoir contract but gains back their name, and lets Dev stay past the last train.
about_author: Xanthe Sterling is the pen name of a former music journalist who spent a decade backstage before turning to fiction. They write stories about people who build families out of strangers and second chances out of wreckage.

chapters.title: Small Safe Steps
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. We meet Noor ghostwriting celebrity memoirs under three pseudonyms, living by strict rules: no bylines, no attachments, no hometowns. A lucrative offer arrives to write pop icon Marisol Vance's memoirs. Noor hesitates—the advance would buy real security—but something about the contract feels off. Emotional beat: cautious hope shadowed by old fear.

chapters.title: The Manager with Familiar Hands
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. At the first interview at Marisol's coastal estate, Noor discovers the manager running the project is Dev Kapoor—the love they abandoned eleven years ago after taking the fall for a stolen song. Dev shows no recognition, or hides it perfectly. Noor almost walks out; the money and the mystery keep them seated. Emotional beat: vertigo, masked as professionalism.

chapters.title: Marisol Sings Her Version
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Noor and Marisol. Marisol recounts her breakout hit 'Lantern Light'—a song Noor wrote and never credited. Marisol tells it sincerely, believing it hers, and her warmth disarms Noor. That night Noor finds the estate's archive room locked but humming with organized secrets. Emotional beat: grief for a self Noor buried to survive.

chapters.title: Postmarked Eleven Years Ago
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. While cataloguing memorabilia, Dev finds an unsent draft of Noor's confession letter, postmarked but returned, hidden in a box of Marisol's early papers. Dev has known for years where the song came from—and protected Marisol anyway. Dev pockets the letter instead of destroying it. Emotional beat: guilt sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Found Family, Borrowed Kitchen
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The estate's staff—housekeeper Rosa, sound engineer Teo, Marisol's teenage sister Luz—fold Noor into late-night kitchen dinners, the first community Noor has let form in years. Dev begins staying for them too, and the two circle each other with old tenderness and new suspicion. Emotional beat: the dangerous warmth of belonging.

chapters.title: The Letter on the Table
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev confronts Noor privately with the letter, demanding to know why Noor disappeared and let Dev believe the worst. Noor admits they took blame for the song's theft to protect someone who then discarded them. Old love reignites into furious honesty. Emotional beat: rupture—truth spoken too late to be painless.

chapters.title: What the Contract Hides
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Digging through the archive legally opened to them, Noor finds proof that Marisol's manager-before-Dev coerced the original credit transfer—and that the current publisher plans to bury the memoir's true chapters. Noor realizes finishing the book honestly will end their career. Emotional beat: the corrupting weight of power, finally visible.

chapters.title: Last Train Before the Festival
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. On festival eve, the publisher offers Noor a fortune to ghost the sanitized version and vanish again. Dev begs Noor to take it and stay safe; Noor refuses. They argue on the platform as the last train leaves without either of them, and Dev asks—not demands—to stay the night. Emotional beat: surrender to vulnerability.

chapters.title: Lantern Light, Sung Back
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, climax. At the Harvest Festival, before thousands, Marisol invites her 'collaborators' onstage. Noor steps up, names themselves as the song's writer, and tells the truth about the coercion while Dev backs the claim with the archived letter. The crowd's roar splits between betrayal and vindication; the publisher's facade cracks publicly. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into claim-staking.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, resolution. The memoir dies as a sanctioned project, but Marisol, freed from her manager's lies, proposes co-writing a new honest album—with Noor credited. Rosa, Teo, and Luz claim Noor as family outright. On the emptying festival grounds, Noor watches the last train go and asks Dev to stay. Emotional beat: quiet, earned homecoming.
